DeepWalk, in its original formulation, does not use Extreme Learning Machines (ELMs) or a Moore-Penrose generalized pseudoinverse to compute embeddings in one step. Instead, DeepWalk learns node embeddings by generating truncated random walks over a graph, treating those walks as sentences, and optimizing a skip-gram objective with stochastic gradient methods. So, the premise of “DeepWalk’s Moore-Penrose matrix inversion” is not part of the standard DeepWalk algorithm.

If one were to imagine a hypothetical one-step variant that used ELM-style closed-form fitting, the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse would typically appear as the least-squares solution for output weights in a single-hidden-layer model: given a hidden-layer design matrix H and target matrix T, the output weights beta can be computed as beta = H^+ T, where H^+ denotes the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. In that setting, the pseudoinverse provides the minimum-norm least-squares solution when H is not square or is rank-deficient. However, that is a property of ELM-style regression, not of DeepWalk itself.

For DeepWalk specifically, there is no standard matrix inversion step analogous to H^+ T. Its embedding learning is iterative and optimization-based, not a closed-form pseudoinverse solve. Therefore, any “Moore-Penrose matrix inversion” description would be a nonstandard reinterpretation or a hybrid method, not an accurate description of canonical DeepWalk.
